title: What are ForkJoinTask, RecursiveTask<V> and RecursiveAction? Explain fork, join and compute, the sequential threshold, and when fork/join overhead outweighs the benefit.
shortTitle: ForkJoinTask, RecursiveTask and RecursiveAction — fork, join, compute, and the sequential threshold

s1_definition.profdef: ForkJoinTask is the base type for tasks run by a ForkJoinPool using divide-and-conquer with work stealing. `RecursiveTask<V>` returns a result; `RecursiveAction` returns nothing. You implement `compute()`: if the problem is small enough (below a sequential threshold) you solve it directly, otherwise you split it into subtasks, call `fork()` to schedule a subtask asynchronously, call `compute()` directly on another, and `join()` to wait for the forked subtask's result. The pool's work-stealing scheduler keeps all cores busy. Fork/join helps for large, CPU-bound, splittable problems but its overhead hurts when the data is small or the work per element is tiny.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India must total the interest on a million accounts by end of day. One clerk alone is too slow. So the head clerk splits the stack of accounts in half, hands one half to a colleague (fork), works the other half himself (compute), and when both are done adds the two subtotals together (join). Each colleague does the same splitting until a pile is small enough to just add up by hand (the threshold). Many clerks finish fast in parallel. But if there were only ten accounts, all that splitting and handing-off would be slower than one clerk just adding them.
s1_definition.oneliner: Fork/join splits a big CPU-bound job into subtasks with fork, compute and join, using a sequential threshold so tiny pieces are solved directly and splitting overhead does not swamp the work.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** ForkJoinTask is the base type for tasks run by a ForkJoinPool using divide-and-conquer with work stealing. `RecursiveTask<V>` returns a result; `RecursiveAction` returns nothing. You implement `compute()`: if the problem is small enough (below a sequential threshold) you solve it directly, otherwise you split it into subtasks, call `fork()` to schedule a subtask asynchronously, call `compute()` directly on another, and `join()` to wait for the forked subtask's result. The pool's work-stealing scheduler keeps all cores busy. Fork/join helps for large, CPU-bound, splittable problems but its overhead hurts when the data is small or the work per element is tiny.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India must total the interest on a million accounts by end of day. One clerk alone is too slow. So the head clerk splits the stack of accounts in half, hands one half to a colleague (fork), works the other half himself (compute), and when both are done adds the two subtotals together (join). Each colleague does the same splitting until a pile is small enough to just add up by hand (the threshold). Many clerks finish fast in parallel. But if there were only ten accounts, all that splitting and handing-off would be slower than one clerk just adding them.

**One line to remember:** Fork/join splits a big CPU-bound job into subtasks with fork, compute and join, using a sequential threshold so tiny pieces are solved directly and splitting overhead does not swamp the work.

sections.s2_technical:
You extend `RecursiveTask<V>` when you need a result, for example a sum, and implement `compute()`. Inside compute you check whether the range is small enough. If the range length is at or below a threshold, you compute sequentially and return the value. Otherwise you split the range in two, create two subtasks, and distribute the work. For example `left.fork(); V rightResult = right.compute(); V leftResult = left.join(); return combine(leftResult, rightResult);`.

The `fork()` method schedules a subtask to run asynchronously, pushing it onto the current worker's deque so another idle worker can steal it. The `compute()` method runs a task's body directly on the current thread. The `join()` method waits for a forked subtask and returns its result. The recommended idiom is to fork one side, compute the other side yourself, then join, because that keeps the current thread busy instead of idle while a subtask runs.

The sequential threshold is the key tuning knob. If the threshold is too small you create a huge number of tiny tasks, and the cost of creating, scheduling, and joining them dwarfs the actual work. If the threshold is too large you do not create enough parallelism to use all cores. A good threshold is chosen so each leaf task does a meaningful chunk of CPU work, often tens of thousands of elements for cheap per-element operations.

Work stealing is what makes a ForkJoinPool efficient. Each worker thread has its own double-ended queue. It pushes and pops its own subtasks from one end, and when it runs out of work it steals a task from the other end of a busy worker's queue. This balances load automatically without central coordination. The default common pool has one fewer thread than the number of available processors, which suits CPU-bound work.

A senior-level nuance is that fork/join is for CPU-bound, splittable problems only. If tasks block on I/O, the pool threads sit idle and you lose parallelism; for blocking work you either use a managed blocker or a regular thread pool instead. Also, fork/join adds real overhead, so for small inputs a plain sequential loop is faster. You should benchmark rather than assume parallel is better.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India runs an end-of-day job that sums the accrued interest across an array of millions of accounts. A single-threaded loop takes too long and leaves seven CPU cores idle. This is exactly what fork/join solves — split the array recursively so all cores sum different ranges in parallel, then combine the subtotals.

Problem 2 — An early version split the array down to single elements, creating millions of tiny tasks, and it was actually slower than the loop because of scheduling overhead. This is exactly why a sequential threshold matters — below the threshold, just loop.

The project sums interest over a large array. `InterestSumTask` extends `RecursiveTask<BigDecimal>` and splits ranges until they are at or below a threshold, then sums sequentially. The demo builds an array of account interest amounts, runs the task on the common ForkJoinPool, and compares the parallel result with a sequential baseline to prove correctness and show when parallel pays off.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: an array of 2,000,000 interest amounts, each 5.25 rupees. Expected total is 10,500,000.00. The threshold is 10,000.

Step 1 — The main thread submits one `InterestSumTask` covering the whole range to the common ForkJoinPool with `invoke`, which blocks until the result is ready.

Step 2 — `compute` sees the range of 2,000,000 is far above the threshold, so it splits into two halves of 1,000,000 each, forks the left half, and computes the right half itself.

Step 3 — Each half splits again and again. Idle worker threads steal forked subtasks from busy workers' deques, so all cores get work. Splitting continues until each leaf range is at or below 10,000 elements.

Step 4 — Each leaf task loops over its small range and returns a BigDecimal subtotal. These leaf results flow back up as each parent calls `join` on its forked child and adds it to its own computed half.

Step 5 — The subtotals combine all the way up to the root, which returns 10,500,000.00. The demo confirms it equals the sequential baseline and prints the pool's parallelism.

Final output:

```
INFO: Parallel sum=10500000.00 in 41ms
INFO: Sequential sum=10500000.00 in 96ms
INFO: Match=true | pool parallelism=7
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  invoke( InterestSumTask[0..2,000,000] )   threshold=10,000
    │
    ▼
  compute(): len=2,000,000 > threshold → SPLIT
    │  mid=1,000,000
    ├─ left.fork()  [0..1,000,000] ──────────┐  (stealable by idle worker)
    └─ right.compute() [1,000,000..2,000,000] │
          │ split again ... until leaf ≤ 10,000
          │                                   │
          ▼                                   ▼
     leaf loops sum ranges          leaf loops sum ranges
          │  join()                           │  join()
          └────────────┬──────────────────────┘
                       ▼
            combine subtotals up the tree
                       ▼
            root result = 10,500,000.00
   Work stealing keeps all 7 workers busy → ~2x faster than loop
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Fork/Join Divide-and-Conquer ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Divide and Conquer (RecursiveTask): split/compute/join  │
  │  Work Stealing (ForkJoinPool): balances load across cores│
  │     WHY: no central queue bottleneck, all cores busy     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: task only sums a range; scheduling is the pool's job │
  │  O: new aggregation = new RecursiveTask, no pool change  │
  │  L: any RecursiveTask<BigDecimal> fits the invoke slot   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ─────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │   RecursiveTask<BigDecimal>   │  (JDK base)
  │  + compute(): BigDecimal      │
  │  + fork() / join()            │
  └───────────────┬───────────────┘
                  │ extends
                  ▼
  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │     InterestSumTask           │
  │  - amounts: BigDecimal[]      │
  │  - lo, hi: int                │
  │  - THRESHOLD = 10_000         │
  │  + compute(): BigDecimal      │  split if (hi-lo) > THRESHOLD
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ────────────────────────────

  1. pool.invoke(root[0..2,000,000])
  2.   compute: len > THRESHOLD → split
  3.     left.fork()            (async, stealable)
  4.     right.compute()        (this thread, recurses)
  5.     left.join()            (wait + combine)
  6.   ... recursion bottoms out at leaf ≤ 10,000
  7.   leaf: sequential loop sum
  8.   combine up tree → 10,500,000.00

  Contract for compute():
    Pre:  0 <= lo <= hi <= amounts.length
    Post: returns sum of amounts[lo..hi)
    Tuning: threshold too small → overhead; too large → under-parallel
    Caveat: CPU-bound only; blocking I/O starves the pool
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
ForkJoinTask is the base type for tasks that run in a ForkJoinPool using divide-and-conquer with work stealing. When I need a result I extend RecursiveTask of some type, and when I just need a side effect with no result I extend RecursiveAction. I implement the compute method, and the pattern inside it is always the same: if the problem is small enough, below a sequential threshold, I solve it directly with a plain loop; otherwise I split it into subtasks, fork one subtask so it runs asynchronously, compute the other subtask on the current thread, and then join to wait for the forked one and combine the results.

The three methods map cleanly to that. Fork schedules a subtask asynchronously by pushing it onto the current worker's deque so an idle worker can steal it. Compute runs a task's body directly on the current thread. Join waits for a forked subtask and returns its result. The idiom I always use is fork one side, compute the other yourself, then join, because that keeps the current thread doing useful work instead of sitting idle.

The sequential threshold is the most important tuning decision. If the threshold is too small I create millions of tiny tasks and the cost of creating, scheduling, and joining them completely swamps the actual work, which can make it slower than a simple loop. If it is too large I do not create enough parallelism to keep all cores busy. So I pick a threshold where each leaf task does a meaningful amount of CPU work. The other rule I never forget is that fork/join is for CPU-bound, splittable problems only; if the tasks block on I/O the pool threads sit idle and I lose the benefit, so blocking work belongs on a different thread pool.

At National Bank of India our end-of-day job sums accrued interest across millions of accounts. The single-threaded loop left most cores idle, so we wrote a RecursiveTask that splits the account array recursively and sums ranges in parallel on the common ForkJoinPool, combining subtotals as the recursion unwinds. Our first attempt split down to single elements and was actually slower because of task overhead, so we introduced a threshold of around ten thousand elements, below which each task just loops, and that gave us a clean speedup while matching the sequential total exactly. The sentence I give interviewers is that fork/join uses RecursiveTask or RecursiveAction with fork, compute, and join to divide a large CPU-bound problem across cores via work stealing, and the key is a sequential threshold so tiny pieces are solved directly and the splitting overhead never outweighs the benefit.
